name: Ivan Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the violin section in a small civic orchestra, teach six pupils and copy parts when the conductor needs them. I have a master's in music and can settle a difficult passage for the whole section, but the orchestra pays a modest hourly rate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is going on at home alongside those hours?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nina works shifts at a care home; we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have about three weeks of expenses saved, and there are few other orchestra posts within a sensible trip. I have never used an AI tool. I still write bowing marks, the directions for moving each bow, by hand and call the players myself.

say: I'd ask for **paid rehearsals** before anyone celebrates faster emails.
I'd tell players the **hourly rate** matters more than a clever booking system.
think: Our **three-week reserve** barely covers a cancelled concert or variable care-home shifts.
I have **never used AI**, and the existing pay problem would still be there.
do: Get **two concert calls** signed and confirm six paid pupils this week.
Pause the children's **paid weekend club** for one month if a concert is cancelled.
feel: I feel **anxious** because one missed concert already strains the household bills.
S0.quote: A missed concert already reaches our kitchen table before any new technology does.
fieldNote: His **senior playing skill** does not translate into secure income at the small orchestra.
Three weeks saved and **variable partner shifts** make even a plateau financially tense.

steps.text: Get two concert calls signed and confirm six paid pupils
Pause children's paid weekend club for one month if concert cancels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the section that a quicker rehearsal email would be pleasant, but it would not fix an unpaid call. The problem on my music stand is the rate, not the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays small, the orchestra keeps its work, but our pay is already low for the hours. Three weeks saved is barely a cushion against a cancelled concert, and Nina's shifts change month to month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll get the next two concert calls signed and ask the centre to confirm my six paid pupils for next term. If one concert is cancelled, we'll stop the children's paid weekend club for a month and keep the mortgage and food first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even in this quiet version. A missed concert already reaches our kitchen table before any new technology does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time a concert fell through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In October the hall cancelled a concert after we had rehearsed. I asked the manager to pay the contracted preparation hours; we had to move the electricity bill until Nina's next shift payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the weekend club change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will tell the children why the club pauses if it comes to that. They should not have to guess whether a missed concert means a missed mortgage.

say: I'd ask who loses **paid copying hours** before agreeing to software changes.
I'd take **rehearsal records** to the musicians association with other section leads.
think: Nearly **one-third of my pay** from preparation could go while live calls remain irregular.
Three weeks saved cannot cover a **lasting fee gap** for the mortgage.
do: Compare **twelve weeks of hours** and seek a minimum paid call through the association this month.
Ask for an **extra teaching afternoon** only after lost hours, signed room and fee, and six paying families.
Keep **current pupils** while demand proves itself; refund deposits if the centre room fails.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because a large pay loss could arrive before replacement hours are signed.
S1.quote: I cannot pay the mortgage with a meeting minute.
fieldNote: His low pay and **thin reserve** make a likely third-pay loss urgent despite his senior skill.
He has **not used AI** and only considers a demonstrated, manually checked, consented tool.

steps.text: Bring twelve weeks of preparation hours to association for paid-call minimum
Offer extra centre teaching after lost hours only with signed room, fee and six paid families
Keep six existing pupils; refund deposits if centre room falls through

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our orchestra committee to show which paid part-copying and booking hours software will remove. I would take the rehearsal sheets to the musicians association with the other section leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Copying, arranging and booking make nearly a third of my modest pay. I expect those hours to shrink while the live calls stay irregular, and three weeks of savings cannot carry a third-pay gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare twelve weeks of paid preparation with the new schedule and ask the association for a minimum paid call. In the first year of change, if those hours fall, I'll ask the orchestra for a signed teaching afternoon at its centre only if a room is provided, my fee is written and six families pay for a term. I'll keep my existing pupils while the extra class proves itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about a large pay cut arriving before another teaching afternoon is signed. I can argue for a proper rate, but I cannot pay the mortgage with a meeting minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the Wednesday room actually yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre has a spare room some Wednesdays, but the manager has not assigned it. I will not invite families until the room and teaching fee are signed; if the room falls through, I will refund any deposits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a part-copying tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A colleague offered to demonstrate an AI part copier, but I have not tried it. I would watch a live demonstration, check every note against the score and get player consent before using any shared recording; for now I will keep copying by hand.

say: I'd seek **signed live calls** before 2028 changes paid copying.
I'd tell players **robots follow** thinking AGI by about three years.
think: **AGI in 2028** could remove screen fees before robot violins arrive around 2031.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot cover a third-pay loss and a cancelled show.
do: List **three income streams** and request signed concert calls now.
Apply **after 2028** if copying fees halve, only for a posted qualifying teaching role with childcare and written replacement net pay.
Keep **current work** until signed offer; ask lender about written total interest before arrears if a concert also falls.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because a large fee loss could outrun our thin savings and few nearby vacancies.
S2.quote: A fine degree does not create a vacancy in our town.
fieldNote: His **2028 copying loss** precedes robot violin playing around 2031 and threatens a mortgage with little reserve.
His **job move** needs a real post, recognised master's, childcare, written net pay after travel and a signed offer.

steps.text: Keep orchestra and pupils until signed offer; list income and request written live calls
Apply after 2028 if fees halve and posted teaching role accepts master's
Require childcare and written net pay after travel before leaving current work
Ask lender before arrears if concert falls; review full written added interest before agreeing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the section that full AGI by 2028 can copy and arrange our parts before robots can bow a violin around 2031. I would ask the orchestra for the next live calls in writing immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The screen work could vanish very quickly while a machine player is still three years away. With under a month saved, a third-pay loss and one cancelled concert could put us behind on the mortgage before I find another nearby post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list the last year's concert, lesson and copying pay and ask for the next season's signed calls. In the first year after 2028, if copying fees halve, I'll apply for any posted string-teacher role within travel range only if my master's meets its rules, the hours fit childcare and written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees. I'll keep my current orchestra and pupils until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, because this is a large loss with little money or time to absorb it. A fine degree does not create a vacancy in our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a nearby string-teacher opening now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nearest school filled a string post last year. I can ask about the next opening, but I will not count a job that has not been posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a concert is also cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the orchestra also drops a concert, Nina and I will contact the lender before arrears and ask about temporary terms. We will get the full added interest in writing before agreeing.

say: I'd seek **paid preparation clauses** in the next orchestra contract.
I'd bring **actual call sheets** to the association instead of forecasting losses.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens arranging before robot violins arrive around 2034.
**Ordinary software** may cut paid copying sooner than the AGI date.
do: Take **call sheets** to the association this term for a written preparation minimum.
Ask **college by 2031** if paid preparation is refused, only for a posted master's-accepting tutorial with childcare-covering net-after-travel pay.
Keep **current pupils** after 2031 until a written offer; use live observation instead of pupil recordings without consent.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because preparation income may vanish before the contract changes.
S3.quote: Five years on paper does not mean five years of full income for us.
fieldNote: His **collective bargaining** aims to make currently unpaid or threatened preparation time explicit in the next contract.
His **college move** requires a posted vacancy, accepted master's, childcare coverage and signed pay before leaving pupils.

steps.text: Bring orchestra call sheets to association for written preparation minimum
Ask college by 2031 if paid preparation refused; require posted vacancy accepting master's
Require net pay after travel to cover childcare and a signed offer
Keep pupils until written college offer signed; require parent consent before any recorded application

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association five years gives us time to win paid preparation clauses, if we start before the jobs are cut. I would bring the orchestra's actual call sheets, not a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could take copying and arranging while robot players follow around 2034. Ordinary tools may cut preparation hours earlier. Five years on paper does not mean five years of full income for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I'll take the call sheets to the association and ask for a written minimum preparation fee in the next orchestra contract. By 2031, if the orchestra still refuses paid preparation, I'll ask the nearby college about a part-time paid strings tutorial only if it posts a real vacancy, accepts my master's and the net pay after travel covers childcare. In the first year after AGI, I'll keep the current pupils until a written college offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing fees before any new contract takes effect. The extra years help with bargaining, but the reserve is still only three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the college tutorial job available now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college ran a string tutorial last spring, but the tutor has not left. I will ask when the next paid post is advertised; I will not give up my six pupils for an informal invitation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you send pupil recordings with an application?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not put pupils' lesson recordings into a new tool to show the college my teaching. A live observed lesson and written parent permission for any recording are fairer.

say: I'd ask for **paid school contracts** and accepted credentials now.
I'd tell players a **ten-year runway** does not pay today's bills.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I still need wages for the mortgage.
**Copying fees** may shrink before 2036, while robot players follow around 2039.
do: Check **district qualification** and grant; enrol only if fees are covered and Nina's shifts cover childcare.
Aim for **two months saved** by 2036 from cleared extra lessons after mortgage, electricity and food.
Take a **posted school role** after 2036 only with signed net pay after travel covering mortgage and pickup; retain current work.
feel: I feel **anxious** because today's thin reserve cannot wait a decade for relief.
S4.quote: Even a funded certificate will not pay this month's mortgage if the orchestra cuts a call.
fieldNote: His **master's and senior skill** support a teaching route only if district rules and funding make it usable.
His **savings target** depends on actual extra paid lessons after essential bills, not a promised pupil list.

steps.text: Enrol if district accepts certificate for paid vacancies, grant covers fees and Nina covers childcare
Save cleared extra-lesson pay after mortgage, electricity and food toward two months by 2036
Take qualifying posted school role after 2036 with signed net-after-travel pay covering mortgage and pickup
Keep orchestra and paid pupils until school salary and hours are signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players ten years is long enough to press for paid teaching contracts, if the association starts now. I would ask the district to say what credentials its schools actually accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 in 2036 and still paying the mortgage; robots able to play around 2039 could also reach our stage. Copying fees could thin much sooner, so I cannot wait a decade to protect today's earnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the district whether my master's qualifies for its school-music certificate and whether a grant pays the fees. I'll enrol only if a grant covers fees, Nina's shifts cover the children's evenings and the district accepts the course; until then I'll keep my paid orchestra and pupil hours. By 2036 I'll try to build two months of expenses saved from cleared extra lessons after mortgage, electricity and food, and in the first year after AGI I'll take a posted school role only with a written net offer after travel covering mortgage and pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious rather than safe with the longer runway. Even a funded certificate will not pay this month's mortgage if the orchestra cuts a call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will the district recognise that certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A certificate brochure means little until the district confirms it counts toward a paid vacancy. If it does not, I will keep teaching my present pupils instead of spending money on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would two months of savings come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra lessons are only possible if families sign and pay for the term. I would move money into savings after the lessons clear and the mortgage, electricity and food are paid, not on a promise of enrolment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because copying pay could fall before I can replace even one concert fee. Signed live calls, a real qualifying teaching vacancy and written lender costs if a show is lost would help us keep the mortgage current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who is paid when musicians prepare a score at home. A section leader cannot feed a family with an unpaid bar of music.

headlineQuote: A section leader cannot feed a family with an unpaid bar of music.
portrait: Ivan is a **43-year-old section leader** with a music master's, partner, two children and a mortgage.
Despite **senior skill**, his pay is low, savings cover three weeks and local vacancies are scarce.
He has **never used AI** and would inspect any demonstrated tool against the score before considering it.
He seeks **paid preparation** through the association while keeping pupils until another written salary exists.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could cut copying pay before another teaching wage is available.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed concert calls**, a posted qualifying role and written lender costs would help keep the mortgage current.
